Q26: Jie Cai, Susan Thibeault
Q25: Exploring the Anti-Fibrotic Effects of Metformin on Vocal Fold Scar
Q27: Objective: This study aims to investigate the inhibitory effects of metformin on vocal fold scarring Methods:  A vocal fold scarring model was established in New Zealand rabbits by injuring the epithelium and lamina propria of vocal fold. Fibrosis was also induced in rabbit vocal fold fibroblasts using TGF-β1. Hematoxylin and eosin(H&E) staining, Masson’s trichrome staining, and immunofluorescence were performed to assess fibrotic changes in vocal fold tissue. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) and Western blotting were used to analyze the expression of fibrosis-related genes and proteins fibroblast. Atomic force microscope (AFM) was used to detect the biomechanical properties of vocal fold fibroblasts.  Results:  H&E, Masson staining, and immunofluorescence revealed that metformin significantly reduced fibrosis in the vocal fold. qPCR and Western blot analyses showed that metformin significantly downregulated the expression of fibrosis-related markers, including COL1A1 and α-SMA, in both scarred vocal fold tissue and TGF-β1-induced fibrotic fibroblasts. Furthermore, AFM analysis demonstrated that metformin decreased the stiffness of fibrotic vocal fold.  Conclusion: Metformin significantly attenuates vocal fold fibrosis in vivo and inhibits TGF-β1-induced fibrotic changes and mechanical stiffness in vocal fold fibroblasts in vitro. These findings highlight metformin’s potential as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of vocal fold scarring.   Keywords: Vocal fold scar; Metformin; Fibrosis; Atomic force microscope

Q26: Deling He, Rebecca E Langhough, Erin Jonaitis, Rachael Wilson, Bruce Hermann, Sterling Johnson, Kimberly Mueller
Q25: Enhanced Sensitivity to Elevated Plasma p-Tau 217 with Proper Name Delayed Recall in the Preclinical Alzheimer's Cognitive Composite
Q27: A pivotal debate in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) concerns the shift toward a biomarker-based diagnostic framework, making it imperative to identify early functional signs that are clinically meaningful and biologically sensitive. Given that language deficits are among the earliest manifestations of AD, we modified the Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC) to address this need by incorporating delayed recall of proper names (unique names of people and places). We analyzed 824 dementia-free participants (mean age ≈ 62 at baseline) from WRAP cohort, stratifying them by plasma p-tau217 levels (using established cutoffs: negative [<0.4 pg/mL; N=539], intermediate [0.4–0.63 pg/mL; N=163], positive [>0.63 pg/mL; N=122]). We constructed six PACC variants: (1) traditional PACC4 (Rey AVLT immediate learning, Logical Memory II [LM II], Digit Symbol, Mini-Mental State Examination [MMSE]); (2) PACC3 (excluding MMSE to mitigate ceiling effects); (3–4) PACC4_PN and PACC3_PN, replacing LM II’s total score with proper-name recall; and (5–6) PACC4+VF and PACC3+VF, adding animal fluency. Cognitive composites were calculated as equally weighed sum of component z-scores. We compared PACC variants` sensitivity (i.e., longitudinal decline rates) associated with plasma p-tau217, using linear mixed models adjusted for age, gender, literacy, and practice (total visits minus one). We showed individuals with positive plasma p-tau217 status exhibited significantly faster cognitive decline across all PACCs. Notably, the proper name enhanced-PACC, especially the parsimonious PACC3_PN, demonstrated the steepest decline—6.4%–19% faster than the traditional and animal fluency-appended versions. Our optimized measure offers critical advantages in clinical utility: an 82% reduction in scoring burden for clinicians (9-point proper names vs. 50-point total LM score), finer semantic memory granularity, and enhanced sensitivity to AD biomarkers. Our findings position proper name-enhanced PACC as a clinically practical and optimal tool for tracking longitudinal cognitive trajectories, highlighting proper names delayed recall as a sensitive marker for AD pathology.

Q25: Combined inhibition of MEK and HDACs improves the cytotoxicity of CD4 and CD8 T cells in NRAS;ASXL1-driven acute myeloid leukemia mice.
Q27: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous malignant blood cancer that occurs mainly in the elderly.  Its treatment outcome is greatly influenced by leukemia-driving mutations and T cell phenotypes at the time of diagnosis. Oncogenic NRAS mutations are associated with both AML progression and multi-drug resistance and treatment failure in AML. We have previously developed a NRAS; ASXL1-driven secondary AML (NA-AML) mouse model, which is characterized by a suppressive immune microenvironment resulting in reduced leukemia killing activities of T cells. Targeting hyperactive RAS/MEK signaling via trametinib (Tra, a MEK inhibitor) attenuates the exhaustion of CD8 T cells and prolongs the survival of NA-AML mice. To further boost the efficacy of Tra, we performed a re-purpose screen of ~2,500 drugs, either approved by FDA for treating various human diseases or currently under clinical evaluation, in the absence or presence of Tra. We identified that quisinostat (Qui), a 2nd generation of HDAC inhibitor, potently inhibited the growth of both mouse and human NA leukemia cells and significantly synergized with Tra in vitro. In addition, combined Tra and Qui (TQ) downregulated AP-1 transcription factors and expression of immune checkpoint ligands (PD-L1/L2, CD80, and CD86) while upregulated expression of MHC I/II in mouse NA-AML cells.   We further validated our results in NA-AML mice. Vehicle (Veh) -treated mice rapidly succumbed to AML and died within 4-5 weeks post-treatment. Tra alone and Qui alone slowed down AML progression and prolonged the survival of leukemia mice, while all TQ-treated mice remained alive ~22 weeks post-treatment. Surprisingly, TQ only provided moderate survival benefits in immunodeficient NSG mice engrafted with NA-AML cells, suggesting an important role of cytotoxic T cells in TQ-mediated AML alleviation. We then analyzed CD4 and CD8 T cells from moribund vehicle-treated mice and age-matched drug-treated mice. TQ decreased the exhaustion of CD4 and CD8 T cells and expanded the activated effector/memory T (Tem) cells. Single-cell RNA-Seq analysis showed increased expression of gene signatures associated with cytotoxicity of Tem cells, including CXCR3 and CXCR5. Consistent with these findings, leukemia: T cell co-culture experiments demonstrated significantly enhanced cytotoxicity of TQ-treated CD4 and CD8 T cells, which appeared to be mediated by increased expression of MHC I and II in AML cells. We are currently pursuing the underlying molecular mechanisms. Our data provide a strong rationale to develop immunotherapies via epigenetic modulation of both leukemia and leukemia-associated T cells.

Q26: Sarah Punshon, CScD, OTR/L, Hannah Ketterhagen, MS, CTRS, Emily Trittschuh, PhD
Q25: Healthy Aging Project-Brain: Personalized Paths to Enhanced Cognitive Health in Older Adults
Q27: Background: There is an increased demand for information on how to support brain health in aging. Research has identified a number of healthy lifestyle behaviors and treatable health conditions that are supportive – and might help prevent cognitive decline. Translating these research study findings into actionable behavioral change for the layperson is important. Healthy Aging Project-Brain, Rehabilitation (HAP-B Rehab) is an adaptation of the original evidence-based Healthy Aging Project-Brain (HAP-B) group facilitated by a rehabilitation professional that is designed to promote healthy lifestyle behaviors for older persons in subacute rehab, residential and/or other inpatient settings.  Methods: HAP-B Rehab was created using the 5-stage group model originally developed by Mildred Ross, OTR. This model was chosen intentionally as activities are sequenced to elicit an organized behavioral response that facilitates learning. Activities for this specific group were selected because they can be tailored in the moment to varying levels of cognitive and physical abilities based on each unique set of group members. This style of group is more inclusive of the varied physical and cognitive abilities of older adults typically treated in subacute rehab, residential, and/or other inpatient settings. Outcomes measured are focused on improving perceived self-efficacy, and include the Perceived Health Competence Scale-2 and the PROMIS 10. The initial pilot of this group is currently in process at the Madison VA Community Living Center and is focused on older adults in subacute rehab.  Results: We will report on our approach to adapting the original HAP-B to develop HAP-B Rehab. We will share outcome measure data from the pilot to date.  Conclusion: Promoting actionable lifestyle behavior change for older adults that is grounded in the evidence requires a tailored approach that meets older adults where they are and can be individualized based on their skills and abilities. HAP-B Rehab is designed to meet this need and allow older adults to practice their personal behavior change goals in a supported environment.

Q26: Elizabeth L. Shaver, Frederique Corcoran, Amanda L. Sullivan, & Rebecca J. Shlafer
Q25: Parental Incarceration and School Psychology: A National Survey of Faculty Members
Q27: Approximately one in 14 children and youth in the United States have had a parent incarcerated at some point in their lifetime. Children with incarcerated parents are at increased risk compared to their peers for poor physical and mental health, academic, social, and behavioral outcomes both in childhood and in adulthood. As primary providers of mental and behavioral health services in schools, school psychologists are positioned to provide support to students with incarcerated parents in the school setting and leverage school-based protective factors. However, meeting this aim requires the proper knowledge and training to do so. The primary goals of this study were to (a) evaluate the state of school psychology curriculum and training practices regarding mass incarceration and parental incarceration; and (b) assess school psychology faculty members’ knowledge, attitudes, and preparation related to the topic of parental incarceration. A total of 173 faculty members (15% of the sampling frame) actively involved in program operations at accredited and approved school psychology graduate programs completed a survey. Results indicated that half of the survey participants included either or both mass incarceration and parental incarceration in their courses. Additionally, school psychology faculty members generally had positive attitudes about the importance to the field of supporting students with incarcerated parents. However, even though school psychology faculty members generally had positive attitudes about the topic, and many are engaging in teaching on it, school psychology faculty members rated their perceived knowledge about parental incarceration as somewhat limited. Qualitative analyses revealed this topic arose most often in relation to fieldwork, including practicum and internship courses and supervision. Findings point to a need for improvements in awareness and knowledge about parental incarceration among school psychology faculty members as well as more deliberate inclusion of mass incarceration and parental incarceration within coursework.

Q26: Keke Long, Haotian Shi, Jiaxi Liu, Xiaopeng Li
Q25: VLM-MPC: Model Predictive Controller Augmented Vision Language Model for Autonomous Driving
Q27: Large AI models like Vision Language Models (VLMs) are powerful at interpreting scenes and reasoning about complex situations. However, they sometimes generate unreliable “hallucinations,” which can be dangerous in safety-critical areas such as autonomous driving.  Our work introduces VLM-MPC, a framework that combines a VLM with a Model Predictive Controller (MPC). The idea is simple: the VLM interprets the driving environment and suggests intentions such as desired speed or following distance, while the MPC ensures safe, smooth control of the vehicle by accounting for dynamics and feedback. Together, they form a closed loop that reduces the risks of overconfident or unstable AI outputs.  We evaluated VLM-MPC using driving datasets and realistic simulations under challenging conditions like rain, fog, night driving, and intersections. Results show that it consistently avoids risky situations, maintains safe distances, and drives more smoothly than relying on a VLM alone.  More broadly, this research demonstrates how combining reasoning models with robust control systems can make AI more reliable and interpretable. It offers a promising path toward safer applications of large models in autonomous driving and other real-world domains where trust and stability are crucial.

Q26: Nicholas Mailloux, Erin Mayfield, Jesse Jenkins, Tracey Holloway, Jonathan Patz
Q25: Comparing the Air Quality and Health Implications of the Inflation Reduction Act and a Net-Zero Pathway
Q27: The transition to a low-carbon economy has the potential to improve health by reducing ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure. We apply a data-driven, systems-level framework that integrates detailed energy system modeling (EnergyPATHWAYS and RIO) with three air quality models (APSCA, COBRA, and ISRM) and exposure–response functions to evaluate cumulative and disparate air quality and health effects associated with climate change mitigation policies and pathways. This approach seeks to comprehensively represent and assess the spatial and temporal distribution and sectoral attribution of impacts, accounting for uncertainty in the choice of air quality model and exposure–response function. Here, we evaluate the health effects of county-level air quality changes in the US from 2022 to 2050 across 15 emission source categories induced by the climate and energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and a more ambitious scenario to achieve net-zero emissions by mid-century. Averaged across the three air quality models, the IRA would prevent 5,860 (95% CI: 5,140–6,570) premature deaths in 2035, largely driven by changes in the electricity and transportation sectors. This equates to 82% of the avoided mortality benefits of the net-zero scenario (7,110 [95% CI: 6,240–7,970] premature deaths) in the same year. By 2050, the IRA prevents 5,140 (95% CI: 4,510–5,760) premature deaths compared to 14,480 (95% CI: 12,700–16,240) under the net-zero scenario. Cumulatively from 2022 to 2050, the IRA has the potential to prevent 115,000 (95% CI: 101,000–130,000) premature deaths from decreased PM2.5 exposure, nearly half (48%) the 239,000 (95% CI: 210,000–268,000) premature deaths prevented under the net-zero scenario. The sectoral distribution of avoidable mortality benefits is largely consistent for all three air quality models. Across all combinations of air quality models and exposure–response functions, avoidable mortality estimates differ at most by a factor of three to five, with most of this variation attributable to the exposure–response relationship.

Q26: Amaka Okori
Q25: The relationship between psychosocial acceptance of disability and vocational rehabilitation engagement services among young adults with disabilities
Q27: Participation and commitment that yield positive outcomes stem from one’s psychological readiness to engage in vocational rehabilitation programs. For an individual with a disability, acceptance of their disability is key to meaningful engagement in rehabilitation services. Theoretically, existing studies support the relationship between disability acceptance and engagement in vocational rehabilitation (VR) services; however, further research is needed to clarify how acceptance influences participation, persistence, and success in VR. Due to evolving rehabilitation practices, youth transition challenges, and post-pandemic recovery, this study is both timely and necessary to advance inclusive, psychosocially informed VR service delivery. The study aimed to evaluate the relationship between disability acceptance and vocational rehabilitation engagement among young adults with disabilities, examining whether autonomy mediates the relationship between disability acceptance and engagement in vocational rehabilitation (VR). Correlation analyses and mediation analyses were used to investigate research questions among 63 young adults with disabilities, aged 18-30, who had received VR services. The findings indicated that a moderately strong, positive relationship exists between the extent to which the participants engaged in VR services and their acceptance of disability. Autonomy did not mediate the relationship between disability acceptance and VR engagement. Implications: A complex set of psychological factors influences engagement. VR professionals can design services to promote choice, self-direction, and collaborative planning, enabling clients to become active agents in their vocational journey.

Q26: Candelaria Bergero, Jing Cheng, Qiang Zhang, Yang Ou, Haewon McJeon, Destenie Nock, Inês Azevedo, Steven J. Davis
Q25: Residual emissions may perpetuate community-scale inequalities of U.S. air pollution in net-zero scenarios
Q27: Achieving net-zero emissions targets reduces GHGs and thus improves air quality, but the magnitude and distribution of these improvements will depend on specific mitigation decisions, such as the amount and location of residual emissions being offset by carbon dioxide removals (CDR). Here, we combine a series of models and datasets to analyze community-scale PM2.5 impacts across the contiguous U.S. of net-zero scenarios with different levels of CDR and thus residual emissions. Both the high- and low-CDR scenarios avoid many PM2.5-related deaths compared to a reference scenario, decreasing from around 200,000 to 160,000 and 130,000 deaths in 2050 in the high- and low-CDR scenarios, respectively. However, the low-CDR pathway leads to lower residual emissions and brings larger health benefits that disproportionately affect non-white and low-income groups. Our results thus suggest that in the absence of concerted transition planning, large-scale CDR deployment could be at odds with the equal distribution of climate mitigation-related health benefits in the U.S.

Q26: Simone Bruno, Beril Mat, Erin L. Schaeffer, Ido Haber, Zhiwei Fan, Tariq Alauddin, Richard F. Smith, Sean P. Prahl, Mackenzie R. Wilcox, Madelynn D. Loring, Peter Achermann, Stefan Beerli, Myles Capstick, Esra Neufeld, Niels Kuster, Larissa Albantakis, Stephanie G. Jones, Chiara Cirelli, Melanie Boly, Giulio Tononi
Q25: Bilateral thalamic stimulation via TES-TI Enhances Sleep Spindle Activity during a Daytime Sleep Episode
Q27: Introduction: Sleep spindles are electroencephalographic (EEG) elements characteristic of non-rapid eye movement sleep. The interaction of the thalamic reticular nucleus with the thalamocortical relay neurons constitutes the neurophysiological mechanism underlying spindle generation. Here, we demonstrate Transcranial Electrical Stimulation with Temporal Interference (TES-TI) ability to enhance spindle activity bilaterally targeting the thalamus.   Methods: 24 participants (age 27.2 ys ± 7.4 ys; 69.6% F) underwent thalamic TES-TI stimulation during daytime naps during N2 sleep. Three envelope frequencies were tested in random order: 10 Hz (TES-TI 10Hz), envelope frequency matched to each participant’s sigma peak (TES-TI Peak), and 0 Hz (TES). Simultaneous 256-channel high-density EEG recordings were performed. Average spectral power in the sigma band (9-16 Hz) across all electrodes was compared before (PRE) and during the stimulation (STIM) using paired Wilcoxon test. Topographic patterns of sigma power changes during the stimulation were assessed using a non-parametric cluster-based permutation test. Spindles characteristics were compared between STIM and PRE using paired Wilcoxon tests.   Results: TES-TI 10Hz stimulation only was associated with a significant increase in sigma power (∆µSTIM-PRE = 0.36 log10µV2, p = 0.042). Cluster-based analysis localized the increase over two frontal and centro-parietal electrode clusters (p = 0.027). TES-TI 10Hz stimulation was also associated with a significant increase in spindle power (∆µSTIM-PRE = 0.035 log10µV2, p = 0.0093).   Conclusions: This study presents the first evidence supporting the successful use of TES-TI during sleep to target the thalamus and enhance sleep spindle activity. Stimulation at a fixed envelope frequency of 10 Hz effectively increased sigma band and individual spindles power, whereas stimulation matched to each participant’s individual sigma band peak did not produce a comparable enhancement. Further research is needed to investigate the cognitive and clinical impact of TES-TI-induced spindle enhancement.

Q26: Jiaqi Yang, Ming Liu, Min Chen
Q25: Beyond Domain Labels: A Unified Knowledge Transfer Framework for Individual Tree Crown Segmentation
Q27: Effectively managing trees is essential for protecting the environment and maintaining healthy ecosystems. A key step in this process is accurately identifying each tree’s canopy from aerial or satellite images. However, most existing methods need a lot of detailed manual labeling for each new area, which takes time and doesn’t work well in unfamiliar places or under different image conditions. To solve this problem, we introduce UniTree, a new method that can detect individual tree crowns in many different regions and image types—without requiring area-specific manual labeling. UniTree includes three main innovations: it learns how to adapt across different landscapes (domain knowledge transfer), across different image resolutions (resolution knowledge transfer), and it learns to find meaningful tree structures using a smart training strategy. We first tested UniTree in Yosemite National Park, where it outperformed other methods in key accuracy measures—improving some by up to 17% in segmentation quality and 34% in detection accuracy. We also explored how changing image bands, model design, and training settings affects performance. Interestingly, we found that simply using more image details or deeper networks doesn’t always help. UniTree was further tested in completely different regions across the U.S., including areas with dense or sparse tree cover and varied landscapes. The results show that UniTree also works reliably in these new and challenging areas. In summary, UniTree offers a scalable and efficient way to map individual trees from remote sensing data, helping support applications like digital forest inventories, ecological research, and land management in the face of environmental change.

Q26: Zheng Ma, Zhenglong Li, Pei Wang, Yong Chen, and Changyong Cao
Q25: The radiometric stability of VIIRS/SNPP RSB over Lake Michigan using a machine learning technique
Q27: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) is a key instrument carried on the JPSS satellite series. It is critically important to understand the VIIRS long-term radiometric stability through the time series analysis. Our previous studies have been focused on regions with deep convective clouds (DCC) and lakes with stable surface such as Salton Sea in California. For other regions like Lake Michigan, however, it is difficult to monitor the radiometric stability of VIIRS directly through  time series analysis from observations because of  relatively strong temporal variations of surface properties due to biological activities and ice and the atmosphere above surface. Therefore, we proposed an alternative method to estimate the radiometric stability of VIIRS visible bands by taking into account the spectral correlations among different bands. This is based on the fact that even if there exist temporal variations on the surface and atmosphere above it, the spectral correlations remain stable in that all bands are observing the same targets. In this study, a machine learning framework is developed to learn the spectral correlations, i.e. predicting one specific VIIRS band from observations of the other 10 visible bands. The models are trained using observations from 2013 and found to have great prediction accuracy. Then the trend of prediction bias for each band is mathematically calculated. While the trend of prediction bias can be regarded as the trend of model prediction minus trend of observation, the model prediction trend is affected by observation trends from the other 10 bands. Sensitivity experiments are carried out with permutations to each predictor band of the predicting models to acquire approximate linear sensitivity coefficients for each predictor band to each target band. The model prediction trends can be approximated by the sum of these coefficients multiplied by their respective observation trends. Therefore, one can get a matrix of 11 equations with 11 unknown variables of observation trends. With the trends of prediction bias calculated from predictions and real observations, one can evaluate the stability of VIIRS bands from the solution of the observations trends. Results over Lake Michigan will be presented. This methodology once proved loose the requirement of stable homogeneous surface, and thus can be applicable to other surface conditions not limited to Lake Michigan.

Q26: Kevin R. Parducho, Zachary T. Morrow, John-Demian Sauer
Q25: Host signaling pathways required for Bacterially-induced Prostaglandin E2 Synthesis
Q27: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is an eicosanoid that contributes to a variety of physiological processes ranging from control of tumor growth to the induction of labor during pregnancy. PGE2 is also essential for optimal CD8+ T-cell priming following L. monocytogenes infection or vaccination. Infection by WT Listeria induces PGE2 production from phagocytic cells. However, our understanding of the host pathways and bacterial factors that regulate PGE2 production remain incomplete. Published data suggests that the host proteins MPGES1, COX-2, and the bacterial protein listeriolysin O (LLO) – which forms pores in the phagosomal membrane for the eventual bacterial escape into the host cytosol – are required for Listeria-induced PGE2 synthesis. Our recent results show that the activity of the calcium-sensitive cPLA2, which canonically initiates PGE2 synthesis via releasing arachidonic acid (a PGE2 precursor) from membrane phospholipids can be inhibited with pyrrophenone and that this decreased PGE2 synthesis from infected macrophages. Given the calcium-sensitivity of cPLA2, we decided to test whether the role of LLO could be due to its ability to induce calcium flux by infecting macrophages with the phagosome-confined Δhly Listeria with concurrent treatment with agents that promote calcium flux. Our data suggests that Listeria access to the cytosol is not required for PGE2 synthesis as simultaneous infection with Δhly Listeria and treatment with an agonist for phagosomal calcium channels phenocopies infection with WT Listeria. Lastly, to determine whether this phenomenon is unique to Listeria infections, we infected macrophages with B. subtilis that artificially express LLO and found similar observations – increased PGE2 synthesis. In sum, these data collectively suggest that Ca2+ flux from bacteria-containing phagosomes – potentially via LLO – can stimulate PGE2 synthesis. This research can help us understand how to modulate the production of PGE2 – a hormone important for cancer immunotherapies and reproductive health.

Q25: Electron Microscopy-based Polyclonal Epitope Mapping for Rhinovirus C
Q27: Human rhinoviruses (RVs) are respiratory pathogens transmitted via droplets or contact. These viruses are primarily responsible for the common cold. Among the three viral species (RV-A, -B, -C), RV-C has been linked to asthma in young children. RV-C has been classified into more than 60 types based on the sequencing of the structural capsid protein. Until now, no approved vaccines or therapeutics are available for RV-C infection, underscoring the urgent need for effective treatments. This study determined the first cryo-EM structure of rhinovirus C, type 41 (RV-C41) at 3.1 Å resolution. Q26: Tong Wang, Yan Liu, Rong Li, Nathan Merrill, Zhongde Wang and Peter Halfmann
Q25: Characterization of transgenic human dipeptidyl peptidase-4 hamsters to study MERS coronaviruses
Q27: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) lacks a tractable small-animal model, limiting studies on pathogenesis and medical countermeasures. Transgenic mice expressing human dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (hDPP4) have been the only available rodent model but do not fully recapitulate transmission dynamics. While wild-type Syrian hamsters are not permissive to MERS-CoV, their proven utility for SARS-CoV-2 research prompted the generation of hDPP4 transgenic hamsters. In this study, we established hDPP4 Syrian hamsters and challenged them intranasally with MERS-CoV (EMC/2012). Trangenic hDPP4 hamsters supported efficient virus replication in the respiratory tract, with high titers in nasal turbinates, trachea, and lungs. To assess transmission, we performed airborne and direct-contact experiments. No transmission occurred across a perforated barrier permitting airflow that prevented direct contact between hamsters, indicating a lack of airborne spread under these conditions. In contrast, co-housing naïve hDPP4 hamsters with infected donors resulted in robust contact transmission, with an extended exposure time yielding 100% infection. Together, these findings establish hDPP4 transgenic hamsters as a practical small-animal model for MERS-CoV that combines efficient respiratory replication with contact-dependent transmission. This model fills a critical gap between mouse and large-animal systems and provides a tractable platform to evaluate medical countermeasures.

Q26: Ziyong Hong, Jiaoyang Jiang
Q25: Cracking the Sweet Code: Mechanistic Insights into Human O-GlcNAcase
Q27: O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic protein modification that regulates essential cellular processes, controlled by the opposing enzymes O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA). Dysregulation of this modification is linked to a wide range of diseases, including cancers and neurodegenerative diseases, highlighting the importance of understanding how these enzymes recognize their substrates. Using integrated techniques, such as small-angle X-ray scattering, cryo-electron microscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigated the structural features of human OGA and its interaction with an important protein substrate. We show that OGA forms a dimer with a rigid catalytic core and flexible domains, and that substrate binding induces major conformational changes on the level of dimerization. These findings provide new insights into OGA substrate recognition and inform strategies to probe and therapeutically target O-GlcNAcylation.

Q25: Genome Editing of Human Leukocyte Antigen Genes in Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells for Immune-Compatible Dendritic Cell Production: A CRISPR Study
Q27: The success of regenerative medicine using allogeneic induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) hinges upon precise genome editing of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes to mitigate the risk of immune rejection. Despite iPSCs' promise in regenerative medicine, HLA mismatch-induced immune rejection poses a significant challenge. Q26: Benjamin J. Smith, Till J. W. Wagner, Nimish Pujara, Hilary A. Dugan, Grace M. Wilkinson, Lucas K. Zoet, Jennifer A. Franck

Q27: Cryptococcus neoformans is a global fungal pathogen contributing to >19% of all AIDS-related deaths, yet the molecular basis of spore  germination, a critical step in pathogenesis, remains poorly understood. Q26: Naviya Schuster-Little, Nic Bollis, Jim Bruce, Mark Scalf, Michael Shortreed, and Lloyd M. Smith
Q25: Characterizing the Epitranscriptome of MALAT1 Using Mass Spectrometry
Q27: Revealing post-transcriptional modifications (PTrMs) of RNA, referred to as the epitranscriptome, is a critical new frontier of biomolecular analysis. While next generation nucleic acid sequencing technologies have made the high throughput analysis of RNA base sequences commonplace and readily available, those approaches are largely limited to the base nucleotide sequence itself, and do not generally enable the identification or localization of RNA modifications. We are using mass spectrometry (MS) as a powerful and versatile technology to identify, localize, and quantify post-translational modifications of native RNAs up to several kilobases in length. One RNA of interest is MALAT1, a long non-coding RNA that is overexpressed in many cancers. Moreover, MALAT1 has reported PTrMs that are known to play a role in the development and progression of many cancers. After linearizing the plasmid, the DNA was transcribed into RNA using in vitro transcription, and the resulting RNA was purified and quantified. The RNA was digested into fragments of 5-30 bases in length using RNase T1. RNA was separated using ion-pairing, reverse-phase, ultra-high-pressure liquid chromatography (IP-RP-HPLC) prior to analysis with tandem MS. We have also determined the limit of detection to be 15 ng, or the equivalent of 5 fmol. Q26: Chuan Luo
Q25: Efficient Computational Design Tool for Metal Additive Manufacturing
Q27: Today, powerful computer tools allow us to design materials and structures that are both strong and lightweight. For instance, if we want to create a structure that doesn’t bend much under certain forces, we can use computer programs to determine exactly where material is needed and where it can be removed. However, turning these idealized designs into real and manufacturable parts isn’t always straightforward. The way we fabricate things often comes with limits. For example, in metal additive manufacturing by laser powder bed fusion, parts that are too big in certain areas can heat up unevenly. This can make them bend, warp, or even crack. To address these challenges, many researchers add complex rules, often geometric constraints, into the design process. However, handling these constraints requires a lot of computing power and often tricky tuning of algorithm parameters, particularly for large-scale problems. In my recent work, I propose a new computational design method that can efficiently manage millions of such manufacturing constraints even on a standard laptop. Unlike traditional approaches, it avoids listing every individual constraint, which greatly simplifies the optimization process. Furthermore, the proposed method is algorithmically simple, adaptive to be extended to different types of manufacturing constraints, and easy to integrate into existing design tools.

Q26: Guy Sobol, David Hershey
Q25: A chemical and mechanical cue integration module governs attachment to plant roots by a soil bacterium
Q27: Background: The genetic programs enabling bacteria to colonize abiotic surfaces are well-characterized, but how these programs function on living tissues is less clear. Plant roots offer an attractive model for studying tissue colonization: they host diverse bacteria, secrete defined chemical signals, and hold significant importance for agriculture. However, plant assays are low throughput and laborious, limiting genetic dissection of colonization. Methods: We developed a system where detached roots can be propagated in liquid medium, bypassing whole plants and allowing genetic analysis of root colonization at scale. We then used a barcoded transposon mutant library to profile genome-wide fitness of Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 during root colonization. Results: Mutants affecting the Gac system, a global regulator of motility, biofilm, and stress tolerance, were enriched in the non-root-associated fraction of our colonization experiment. Surprisingly, targeted mutants disrupting the Gac system showed no adhesion or growth defects in direct colonization experiments. These results suggest that Gac signaling promotes bacterial retention on roots by reducing motility and delaying dispersal, rather than mediating adhesion or detoxifying root-secreted compounds. In contrast, flagellar structural mutants displayed hyper-adhesive phenotypes, suggesting that these mutations mimic the obstruction of flagellar rotation during surface contact. Although Gac-regulated pathways are well known, its activating signals are not. Using transcriptional reporters, we show the Gac system is activated by both impaired flagellar function and root-secreted compounds broadly used by the plant to facilitate host-microbe interactions. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that the Gac system integrates mechanical and chemical cues to drive root colonization, revealing a regulatory logic for surface persistence that may extend to other host-microbe interactions.

Q26: Yashar Makhtoumi1, Yanhua Xie, Tyler Lark
Q25: Field Level Mapping of Irrigated Land across the US
Q27: %80 of the US water use comes from agriculture. Growing demand for freshwater, due to population growth as well as increasing uncertainty of extreme climate conditions necessitate better understanding of the water use in agricultural fields which will lead to a more sustainable water management. In recent decades, advances in remote sensing helped researchers to study water use in agriculture. The ability to remotely sense water usage at field/farm level is an opportunity towards better understanding the water use. To this end, we will develop a novel irrigation mapping approach to identify irrigated fields across the US. Irrigation results in different crop phenology compared to rainfed agriculture which results in different spatio-temporal vegetation distribution such as differences in greenness and biomass. Our approach will leverage shape, texture, location, neighbor as well as spectral information with underlying assumption that irrigation has a positive effect on crop growth throughout the field. For comparison purposes, we will also create two other CONUS-wide irrigation maps based on LANID (Xie et al. 2021) and a few field boundary datasets. The first map is LANID-based field level irrigation map where fields’ irrigation status is determined using geospatial techniques. The second map is also LANID-based; however, the fields’ irrigation status is classified using ML methods. And the last map is based on a novel methodology which will leverage new variables and field level spectral behavior as opposed to pixel level. The result will be continental US maps that represent irrigated farms with delineated boundaries. All the maps are based on Landsat imagery.

Q26: Samuel T. Salemink-Harry, Edison Huang, Nimish Pujara
Q25: Pickup of particles by wave-swash interactions
Q27: In the swash zone, waves are responsible for transporting substantial quantities of sediment and dissolved materials. The interaction between an incoming wave and the swash generated by the preceding wave can result in significant vertical accelerations within the water column. We investigate how these interactions lead to the pickup of aluminum particles in a laboratory setting. Pairs of solitary waves, varying in amplitude between 0.03 m and 0.12 m, are generated to create wave-swash interactions within a 39 m long, 1 m wide, and 0.3 m deep wave flume. The waves subsequently shoal and break on a 1:10 sloping beach. A 6.35 mm wide and tall aluminum hollow cylinder located 0.3 meters from the still water line on the beach (corresponding to 0.03m water depth). The particle is confined to vertical motions by a vertically oriented wire and rests 3mm above the sloping beach. The subsequent motion of the particle is monitored by a high-speed camera through a glass side wall. The initial wave does not pickup the particle; however, the subsequent wave initiates pickup for certain wave heights and separations. The observed pickup is influenced by the generated wave heights and separation time, resulting in varying maximum pickup distances of the particle.

Q26: Ximeng Wang; Junliang Liu; Kieran Rivers; Ricardo Vidrio; Yuhan Tong; Adrien Couet; Jennifer Choy; Alexander Kvit; Yongfeng Zhang
Q25: Density Functional Theory Study of Charge Distribution at Metal-ZrO2 Interface
Q27: Conventional corrosion theories often assume homogeneous oxidation. However, oxides formed during oxidation often contain nanoscale metallic inclusions (NMI). The presence of NMIs, especially at high densities, may disrupt the transport of charged species and lead to inhomogeneous oxidation. To investigate the influence of NMIs, Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations are employed to investigate charge distribution across the interface between various metals (e.g., Au, Ag, Al) and ZrO₂. The influence of the metal-oxide interface can extend to hundreds of nm at low doping levels, implying that even small-sized NMI can affect charge transport in oxides significantly.

Q26: Quentin Perraud, Vanessa Sperandio
Q25: Repurposing sulfapyridine to target virulence gene expression in enterohemorrhagic E. coli
Q27: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) is a food-borne pathogen that can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a life-threatening condition. The use of antibiotics for the treatment of EHEC infections is controversial since it often causes an increase in production of Shiga toxin, the main contributor to HUS.  A different approach for the handling of EHEC infection would be to target virulence by hijacking bacterial signaling systems controlling the attachment of bacteria to the intestinal epithelium. The main driver of EHEC’s attachment is a type III secretion system encoded on a pathogenicity island called the locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE). This type III secretion system’s expression is tightly regulated, a fact that has been exploited for the design of virulence inhibitors.  Considering the challenges in developing novel antimicrobial drugs for niche use, we have turned toward re-purposing already FDA-approved molecules as potential virulence modulators by evaluating structural analogues of hits identified through a large chemical library performed in our lab. Q26: Ximeng Wang #, Ziang Yu#, Yachun Wang* and Yongfeng Zhang*
Q25: Multiscale Study of helium diffusion in Ni-Cr alloys: Short-range trapping versus long-range channeling
Q27: Ni-Cr alloys are widely employed as structural materials in fast nuclear reactors but are vulnerable to high-temperature helium (He) embrittlement (HTHE) under fast neutron irradiation. A comprehensive understanding of He diffusion in Ni-Cr alloys, which governs the kinetics of HTHE, is therefore essential for developing resilient materials and preventing failure. In this study, we reveal the underlying mechanisms of He diffusion in pure Ni and Ni-Cr alloys by integrating density functional theory (DFT) with atomistic kinetic Monte Carlo (AKMC) simulations. Our findings uncover a non-monotonic dependence of He diffusivity on Cr concentration, contradicting the monotonic trends predicted by DFT-parameterized theories. At low Cr concentrations, He diffusion is dominated by short-range trapping, characterized by multiple trapping sites and a distinct mechanism within the first nearest neighbor of Cr, differing from that in pure Ni. At high Cr concentrations, these local traps become interconnected, forming long-range fast diffusion channels that enhance He mobility. The competition between localized trapping and extended channeling results in a diffusivity that first decreases, then increases with rising Cr content. These atomic-scale insights offer critical guidance for the design of radiation-tolerant Ni-based alloys. Moreover, the combined DFT-AKMC methodology and the concept of random walk diffusion through interconnected energy basins present a broadly applicable framework for studying transport phenomena in disordered systems.

Q26: Mia E. Phillips, William R. Morrison III, Alison R. Gerken, Emily N. Bick
Q25: Sound & Vibration in Insect Pest Detection
Q27: Insect pests are major threats to agricultural products at all stages of the supply chain. Insects can destroy crops in fields and can infest our stores of dried products like corn and wheat. These infestations result in devastating economic loss. Early detection of these pests allows for timely intervention and prevention of further damage to agricultural commodities. Conventional methods can be time-consuming and often require close inspection of the field or storage facility. This can be avoided, however, by using remote sensing devices that detect the presence of pests and alert farmers or managers to infestations. Vibroacoustic sensors have been shown to detect the sounds and vibrations produced by pest insects in various agricultural products. Here, we present three projects assessing the potential for vibroacoustic recording as a means of passive detection of pest insects. First, we recorded vibrations produced by three Coleopteran stored product pests in small masses of dried whole wheat. We found clear differences in the vibrations produced by each species, opening the possibility for automated detection and identification of these pests. Next, we tested the ability of inexpensive acoustic recorders to detect emergences of adult Plodia interpunctella moths, an important stored grain pest. Last, we present our current work at UW Madison, where we test the ability of the Insect Eavesdropper (an invention of the Bick Lab) to detect a variety of pest species in numerous crop types. Q26: Bethany Korwin-Mihavics, Wenxuan Dong, Chi Yan, Kate Stack, Gillian Hughes, Kevin Schwartz, Margaret Alexander
Q25: Nutritional and microbiota affects on Cryptosporidium infection
Q27: Malnutrition is a major contributor of susceptibility to severe infection with Cryptosporidium, an intestinal protozoan parasite, especially in young children. Diet is known to shape the intestinal microbial community which often changes immune behavior. Despite a clear association between malnutrition and microbiota composition, the impact of malnutrition-associated microbiota on susceptibility to Cryptosporidium infection has not been explored. I hypothesized that diet-associated microbiota modulate the immune response to C. parvum. To test the effects of the microbiota on infection severity, antibiotic pretreatment and protein malnutrition models were used. Broad-spectrum antibiotics or well-nourished or undernourished diets were administered beginning 7 days before C. parvum infection. The protein malnutrition model consisted of 20% protein diet for well-nourished controls and an isocaloric 7% protein diet for undernourished mice. Parasite shedding in the malnutrition model differed with respect to background microbiota and sex. Increased parasite shedding was more pronounced in males than in females, but this was only observed in mice from one animal facility while there was no difference between well-nourished and undernourished male mice from a second facility. Diet and sex may play a role in shaping the microbiota and the response to parasite infection.

Q26: Eric C. Lin, Yiwei Dong, Patrick Barros Tiburcio, Christopher M. Domes, Wan-Ju Li
Q25: Enhancing Skeletal Regeneration by Modulating Stem Cells Through Gata6
Q27: The maintenance of skeletal health is fundamental to preserving mobility, independence, and quality of life in older adults. Age-related deterioration of musculoskeletal integrity is a growing global concern, contributing to frailty, reduced physical capacity, and increased mortality risk.  Skeletal tissue aging causes decreased bone mass and impaired fracture healing. Periosteal stem cells (PSCs) expressing paired-related homeobox 1 (Prrx1) are essential for bone remodeling and fracture repair. Our previous work identified GATA6, a zinc-finger transcription factor of the GATA family, involved in the regulation of human MSC aging. Building on this finding, our current study targets Gata6 to enhance PSC function in a mouse model. We generated Prx1-CreERT2-EGFP;Gata6flox/flox;Ai14 mice for this study. PSCs isolated from control and Gata6-cKO mice contained mostly a cell population expressing the surface markers Sca1 and CD29. Furthermore, Gata6-cKO PSCs demonstrated increased proliferation rates and higher mitochondrial membrane potential compared to controls. Q26: Tae Hyun Lee, Doug R. Braun, and Tim S. Bugni

Q26: Haylee L. Hamilton, Rachel S. Becker, Matteo T. Meyer, Sandhya Ramachandran, Caelan Wright, Marcelo R. Vargas, Mariana Pehar
Q25: FABP7 as a therapeutic target in Alzheimer’s disease

Q26: Kerrie Fanning, PhD, Margaret Kerr, PhD, & Julie Poehlmann, PhD
Q25: Observed caregiver disrupted communications and parental reflective functioning within families experiencing parental incarceration
Q27: Research shows that parenting behaviors and early parent-child relationships significantly impact children's development (Cooke et al., 2022). Generally, sensitive and responsive parenting is linked to more positive child outcomes, while insensitive, withdrawn, or harsh behaviors, termed disrupted communications, are associated with worse child outcomes. Two measures currently exist for assessing disrupted communications: the Atypical Maternal Behavior Instrument for Assessment and Classification (AMBIANCE/AMBIANCE-Brief; Bronfman et al., 2009/2014; Cooke et al., 2020) and the Fearful/Frightening (FR) coding scale (Main & Hesse, 1992/2005); and Jacobvitz et al. (2024) recently proposed an extension of the FR scale, the anomalous/frightening scale. A new measure, the Observed Disrupted Adult-Child Communications (ODACC) rating scale (Fanning & Poehlmann-Tynan, 2020) was developed based on review of existing research, observations of caregiver-child interactions, and the AMBIANCE and FR measures. It was developed to complement the Early Relational Assessment (Clark, 2014), a global measure of negative and positive interactions, and is designed for use in clinical practice and situations where video recording is not feasible or available (e.g., parent-child visits in carceral settings, in-vivo coding). The ODACC is shorter and requires less training compared to existing measures. Preliminary evidence suggests the ODACC is associated with children’s cortisol levels and attachment security and with caregiver depression symptoms (Fanning et al., 2019/2021). In a small sample of caregiver-child dyads with a parent currently incarcerated (N=14), the current study assessed relations between the ODACC scores with parental reflective functioning (PRF), or caregivers’ ability to take the child’s perspective while holding their own perspective and behaviors in mind (Luyten et al., 2017). Analyses suggest that ODACC scores were related to caregivers' PRF, with higher PRF scores on the Parental Reflective Functioning Questionnaire (Luyten et al., 2017) linked to fewer affective communication errors on the ODACC. This study provides additional preliminary evidence for the ODACC's concurrent validity.

Q26: Laura Prieto, Maria Mora Pinzon, Kristen Pickett
Q25: What Do They Care about? Priorities of Care Partners in a Latine Parkinson Disease Community
Q27: Partners, family, or friends of people with Parkinson disease (PD) are a critical part of the care team and often assist with several daily activities to promote independence for the person with PD. Latine people with PD may even be more reliant on care partner support than other racial or ethnic groups, but little is known about the experience of Latine care partners of people with PD. Participation in the study consists of two telephone or video calls, each lasting approximately one hour in the participant’s preferred language (English or Spanish).  Thirteen care partners have consented to participate, and nine care partners (56.8 ± 11.8 years old; 8 females, 1 male) have completed all parts of the research study. Most participants (n = 7) provided 3 or more days/week of support. Q26: Luoliang Xu
Q25: Divergent Ontogenetic Thermal Habitat Shifts Reveal Hidden Risks of Warming for Lake Fishes
Q27: Climate change is altering lake ecosystems worldwide, yet projections of fish responses typically rely on adult thermal preferences and summer-averaged temperatures. Such approaches overlook two critical complexities: that thermal optima differ across life stages, and that climate warming progresses unevenly across seasons. We addressed these gaps by modeling daily temperature profiles for 12,688 lakes across the Midwestern United States and evaluating changes in thermal habitat for 60 freshwater fish species spanning cold-, cool-, and warm-water guilds. For each species, we quantified “preferred days” for both growth and reproduction (egg development) and compared habitat availability between an early baseline period (1980–2000) and a recent warming period (2001–2021). Across all thermal guilds, reproductive habitats declined more sharply than growth habitats, with losses occurring even among warm-water species. Cold-water fishes were most vulnerable, with nearly all populations losing suitable habitat for both growth and reproduction. By contrast, many cool- and warm-water species exhibited divergent responses—gains in growth habitat but simultaneous declines in reproductive habitat. This ontogenetic decoupling reduced the number of lakes that provide seasonally suitable conditions for complete life cycles, underscoring reproduction as the critical bottleneck for population persistence. The results challenge the prevailing assumption that climate warming will consistently favor warm-adapted species and highlight the limitations of management strategies that focus on adult growth potential alone. Conservation planning must therefore adopt an ontogenetically comprehensive perspective, incorporating life-stage-specific thermal needs and seasonal dynamics to identify true climate refugia for whole life cycle and sustain inland fisheries under ongoing warming.

Q26: R. Gaur, R. M. Churchill, V. Fernandez, and the DESC team
Q25: Exploring the space of omnigenous stellarators using the DESC code
Q27: Stellarators are 3D toroidal magnetic confinement devices that are used to achieve nuclear fusion. However, there exists billions of possible 3D stellarator shapes. We draw trends that will be useful for designing reactor-scale stellarators of the future.

Q26: Kyle Fouke, Andrea Dutton, Mayandi Sivaguru, Charles Kerans
Q25: Last Interglacial Sea-Level Variability Recorded in Fossilized Coral Reefs in the Bahamas-Caicos Archipelago
Q27: Sea level records within sedimentary archives allow us to improve our understanding of past sea level-ice sheet interactions during past warm periods that help to provide informed predictions of future sea-level rise. Coral reef deposits from the most recent warm period called the Last Interglacial (LIG), from ~129-116 thousand year ago, suggest complex sea-level variability as evidenced by regional unconformity and/or hiatus surfaces that vertically separate individual reef units. There is debate as to whether this observation is evidence of a sea-level fall or perhaps a rapid rise. Here, I provide new observations of a regional erosional unconformity surface across the Bahamas and Turks and Caicos Islands to determine if this surface represents a brief sea-level fall that exposed the reef. This project is the first to utilize super resolution autofluorescence (SRAF) microscopy to characterize the alteration (diagenesis) from marine and freshwater sources in coral reef deposits. This new approach was successful in documenting the first conclusive evidence of a subaerial exposure within the LIG fossil reefs that must have formed from a sea-level fall followed by sea-level rise. Radiometric ages of the fossil corals reveal that this sea-level fall with the LIG warm period lasted less than 1.5 thousand years and SRAF data constrain the magnitude of the sea-level fell to 1.3-2.7 m. This sea-level variability illuminates rapid changes that occurred in polar ice sheet volume within a past warm period. Future work will include globally distributed sites that include the Seychelles and Western Australia. Including these sites will help determine the geographic extent, precise timing, and local magnitudes of rapid sea-level change (i.e., potentially in excess of 1 m/century) during the LIG to constrain the potential rate of sea-level response to ice sheet growth and retreat.

Q25: Validation of a Mouse Model of Dysfunctional Oropharyngeal Swallowing-Induced Aspiration Pneumonia
Q27: Backgrouds: Nerve injured animal models help elucidate the role of individual nerves in swallowing function.
